62.0208/58.7188 us at T128 and 1957.6364/1924.3356 us at T1024. Group4 SPM is
1907.5736 us at T1024. At T1024, private-L2→LLC PUTX rises from 26,958 to
371,613; group4 reduces it to 30,214. SPM aggregate-core-time attribution is
40.51% softmax/rescale, 22.00% QK, and 21.21% PV. These are ROB-head/idle-PC
attribution bins, not causal saved-cycle estimates or exact phase wall times.

IMPORTANT baseline audit: the current cache reference kernel retains 25,600
unused `clock_gettime` calls in the T1024 ROI despite `ft=nullptr`, accounting
for about 2.98% of attributed core time. Also, private L2 uses TreePLRU in
baseline and LRU in SPM because the existing Ruby config selects LRU when
SPM ways are eligible. Therefore the observed 1.0173x is not yet a clean
CacheFlex gain. Next: separately remove unused baseline timers and use LRU
in both variants, then rerun. Neither change was made in this profiling task.
Historical sections below may predate these findings.

title: Purpose
text:
This repository is the multicore CacheFlex/gem5 development tree. The immediate
goal is to obtain a controlled W7 GEMM comparison between a coherent-cache ACL
baseline and an SPM-optimized version, with detailed ROI, DRAM, Ruby, and Garnet
counters.

The intended architectural split is:

- `../cacheflex_micro` is authoritative for CacheFlex behavior inside the CPU
  core: O3 pipeline behavior, the dedicated SPM LSQ, SPMCP/SPMLD ordering, and
  RAW/WAR shadow-table semantics.
- This repository is authoritative for the multicore extension: the
  `MESI_Three_Level_SPM` Ruby protocol, per-core private SPMs, directory
  controllers, Garnet, coherence fixes, and multicore statistics.
- The active CPU model for the comparison is `DerivO3CPU`, not `NeoverseV2`.

Do not replace the micro shadow-table behavior with a global fence or a rule
that stalls every SPMLD behind every older SPMCP. The micro implementation is
address-aware and blocks only overlapping SPM slots/ways, with sequence-number
filtering and complementary WAR protection.

title: Current source state
text:
### O3 core port

All 60 files present under `../cacheflex_micro/gem5/src/cpu/o3` were copied into
`gem5/src/cpu/o3`. This brought over the complete micro O3 implementation,
including:

- separate regular and SPM LSQ units;
- SPM load/store port accounting;
- the sequence-numbered `spmShadowTable`;
- address-aware SPMCP-to-SPMLD RAW blocking;
- pending-load tracking and SPMCP WAR deferral;
- wakeup/replay when SPM copy responses complete;
- squash, retirement, and cleanup behavior.

Six newer files remain only in the multicore tree:

- `IQUnit.py`
- `SMT.py`
- `bac.cc`, `bac.hh`
- `ftq.cc`, `ftq.hh`

The imported micro `SConscript` does not select these files, so they should not
affect the active O3 model. Do not delete them without checking whether another
build target uses them.

The core is no longer byte-for-byte identical to the micro tree because two
narrow compatibility adaptations were required for this repository's newer
gem5 infrastructure:

1. In `gem5/src/cpu/o3/FuncUnitConfig.py`, old `IprAccess` is mapped to the
   current `System` OpClass. It remains a single non-pipelined FU with latency
   three.
2. In `gem5/src/cpu/o3/BaseO3CPU.py`, `TournamentBP` is wrapped by the newer
   `BranchPredictor(conditionalBranchPred=...)` interface. The conditional
   predictor remains TournamentBP.
3. In `gem5/src/arch/arm/regs/misc.cc`, `TPIDR_EL0` is kept serializing. The
   newer ARM ISA normally emits non-serializing MSR/MRS forms for this register,
   but the imported micro O3 lacks the newer misc-register dependency machinery;
   serializing it preserves the micro tree's MSR/MRS ordering and prevents a
   following TLS read from observing the pre-write value.
4. In `gem5/src/mem/ruby/structures/CacheMemory.cc`, the ISA's 10-bit logical
   SPM set is folded onto the implemented private-cache set count when checking
   and accessing an SPM slot. The matched 256 KiB, 16-way cache has 256 sets;
   retaining all ten logical bits incorrectly rejected valid slots such as
   logical set 518, which physically maps to set 6.
5. In `gem5/src/cpu/o3/lsq.cc`, SPM response tags are also recovered from the
   returning request flags in the common LSQ response entry point. The newer
   Ruby sequencer can return through its shared CPU response path rather than
   `SpmPort::recvTimingResp`; central classification preserves the micro O3's
   separate-SPM-LSQ completion and shadow-table wakeup behavior.
6. In `gem5/src/cpu/o3/BaseO3CPU.py`, `spm_port` is included in the inherited
   cached-port list. This restores the multicore tree's Ruby connection for the
   micro O3's dedicated SPM LSQ port; without it, regenerated configuration
   metadata leaves `system.cpu.spm_port` unconnected.
7. In `MESI_Three_Level_SPM-L0cache.sm`, dedicated SPM data/ack responses are
   accepted without changing any stable or transient coherent L0 state. Once
   the dedicated CPU port is connected, an SPM copy response can overlap a
   normal miss to the same source line; the response callback is independent
   and must not cause an invalid transition while that miss is in flight.
8. In `gem5/src/cpu/o3/lsq.cc`, once the micro O3 captures an SPMCP's encoded
   destination from its store-data operand, it records that destination in the
   multicore Request's dedicated SPM metadata. Source-address translation then
   cannot overwrite the destination; Ruby installs the private SPM slot at the
   encoded address instead of aliasing the coherent source line.
3. In `gem5/src/cpu/o3/fu_pool.cc`, the removed generated-parameter iterator
   typedefs `FUDDiterator` and `OPDDiterator` are replaced with C++ `auto`
   iterators. The loops and functional-unit construction order are unchanged.
4. The newer multicore `Request` names (`SPMLD`, `SPMST`, `SPMCP_FETCH`, and
   `SPMWB_STORE`) provide aliases for the names used internally by the micro
   O3 port (`SPM_LOAD`, `SPM_STORE`, `CP_TO_SPM`, and `SPM_WRITEBACK`). The
   aliases retain the multicore protocol's existing flag values. The micro
   request-port SPM identification hook is also retained, and an explicit
   explicit boolean conversions are used for the newer `RefCountingPtr` API.
5. The micro O3 packet response tags are retained. At the multicore boundary,
   `SpmPort` derives the copy-response versus SPM-load/store-response tag from
   the existing multicore `Request` flags before handing the packet to the
   micro LSQ response and shadow-table logic.
6. The O3 trace probes use this repository's newer `ProbeListenerObject`
   header and `connectListener` ownership API. This affects optional tracing
   integration only, not pipeline or SPM ordering behavior.
7. `DynInst::setMiscRegOperand` retains the newer register-class handling for
   immediate non-speculative updates of non-serializing miscellaneous
   registers. This is required for ARM `MSR`/`MRS` sequences such as glibc's
   `TPIDR_EL0` TLS setup; deferred commit behavior remains in place for
   serializing registers.

These are API translations, not intended microarchitectural changes.

### Ruby and multicore behavior

The `MESI_Three_Level_SPM` Ruby protocol and Garnet implementation remain from
`cacheflex_mc`; they were not replaced by micro-repository files. Existing
multicore coherence changes, SPM counters, and NoC counters must be preserved.

The active configuration uses one private SPM per CPU, one L2 controller per
CPU, and one directory per CPU. The benchmark accepts 1, 2, 4, or 8 CPUs.

### GEMM benchmark

Relevant files:

- `benchmarks/acl_sve_gemm/gemm_driver.cpp`
- `benchmarks/acl_sve_gemm/acl_kernel.cpp`
- `benchmarks/acl_sve_gemm/build.sh`
- `benchmarks/cacheflex_spm_gemm/build.sh`
- `benchmarks/cacheflex_spm_gemm/run_matched_acl_garnet.sh`
- `benchmarks/cacheflex_spm_gemm/run_mesi3_spm_garnet.sh`
- `benchmarks/cacheflex_spm_gemm/run_w7_core_sweep.sh`
- `scripts/analyze_gemm_epochs.py`

The active benchmark has been converted to FP16 and uses the micro repository's
two-way-unrolled 8-by-3VL fused SVE kernel. At 512-bit SVE, one output tile is
8 by 96. Row-major zero-valued A and B inputs are initialized before the ROI
using `m5_read_file`; their packing is performed by the paper's pack routines
inside the measured ROI.

The driver has subsequently been aligned with the paper's actual VL=4 W7
inputs, `v1_fused` and `v3_fused_vl4`: A and B enter as row-major matrices,
the ROI loop order is K -> m0 -> pack A -> n0 -> pack/copy B -> fused kernel,
and W7 uses KC=256 and MC=784.  Packing now executes inside the ROI.  The
multicore-only additions are contiguous M-tile partitioning, synchronization,
and chronological per-N-panel statistics epochs.  Fresh result directories
use the `derivo3paperdriverpf` tag so they cannot be confused with the earlier
prepacked-driver measurements.

Current SPM behavior:

- B is copied with the single-line `SPMCP_64_IMM` instruction; SNAP/move
  semantics were reverted.
- Ruby now follows the CacheFlex state table's destructive source-move path:
  an I-state source uses `GETS_SILENT`, while a resident S/SS, E/EE, or M/MM
  source is first recalled from L0 when necessary, then released with
  PutS/PutE/PutM; the destination enters X only after data or Put-Ack.
- `num_spm_ways` defines the low ways software may dynamically claim. Those
  ways remain normal coherent capacity until an SPM install marks a slot as
  scratchpad, are excluded from coherent allocation/replacement while claimed,
  and return to coherent capacity on `SPM_release`. A coherent occupant is
  physically migrated to any free unclaimed way in its set during a claim.
- No batched or multicast SPMCP instruction has been implemented yet.
- Each K row occupies three 64-byte SPM ways.
- The staging loop is barrier-free and relies on the micro shadow table.
- The SPM kernel wraps a speculatively generated set-256 address back to set
  zero, permitting a natural 256-row W7 K tile instead of a 255+1 split.
- Work is partitioned into contiguous M-tile ranges per thread.
- The SPM assembly kernel accepts a count and sweeps the thread's contiguous
  M blocks internally, amortizing kernel setup.
- The VL=4 micro repository's two-way software-pipelined FP16 K loop is used
  through `benchmarks/acl_sve_gemm/fp16_kernel.cpp`. VL=8 and VL=16 tile-shape
  kernels have not been ported into the multicore harness.
- Each core still copies the same B panel independently. This is expected to
  increase replicated traffic at higher core counts until batch/multicast copy
  support is designed and implemented.

Both baseline and SPM runners now select `DerivO3CPU` and explicitly match the
paper sweep's core-side parameters per CPU:

- fetch/decode/rename/commit width: 5;
- dispatch/issue/writeback width: 8;
- ROB: 128 entries;
- IQ: 80 entries;
- regular LQ/SQ: 32/48 entries;
- physical integer registers: 128;
- physical float/vector registers: 192;
- vector predicate registers: 64;
- regular cache ports: 2 load, 1 store;
- SPM ports: 2 load, 1 store;
- CPU clock: 2.5 GHz (system clock: 1.5 GHz);
- SVE: 512 bits.

The Ruby cache geometry now capacity-matches the paper in both runners: Ruby
L0I/L0D (architectural L1) are 64 KiB, 4-way; Ruby L1 (private CacheFlex/L2)
is 512 KiB, 8-way; and Ruby L2 (LLC/L3) is 4 MiB, 16-way, with 64-byte lines.
Three Ruby-L1 ways are reserved only in the SPM run. Ruby's L0 stream
prefetcher is enabled in both variants. This is not the paper's exact classic-
cache Stride/AMPM/BOP prefetch chain, which Ruby does not provide.

The initial capacity-matched SPM run panicked after ROI entry because raw SPM
slot `0x1d80` aliased the SE-translated physical instruction line for virtual
PC `0x401d80`. Ruby then coalesced the SPMLD and instruction fetch and returned
zero SPM data as instruction bytes. `Sequencer.cc` now canonicalizes all Ruby-
side SPM slot addresses into the reserved `0x60000000` namespace while keeping
the ISA's low 19-bit way/set/offset encoding. The fixed one-core W7 run passes
with Ruby prefetching enabled and completes all 8,448 issued SPMCPs.

The capacity/core-matched one-core FP16 W7 ROI totals are 1,603,625,200 ticks
for baseline and 1,614,376,000 ticks for SPM, or 0.993x baseline performance.
This is much closer to, but does not reproduce, the paper's 1.029x VL=4 W7
speedup. Ruby still does not implement the paper's exact Stride/AMPM/BOP chain.

The exact paper VL=16 W7 tile drivers were also run on the original micro
repository's classic three-level cache hierarchy and prefetch chain. The
baseline completed in 672.4 us (611.35 GFLOPS) and SPM in 569.5 us
(721.74 GFLOPS), a 1.181x speedup. This closely reproduces the paper's
hardcoded 602.86 versus 706.44 GFLOPS, or 1.172x. The same drivers on this
repository's Ruby hierarchy produce 584.1 versus 534.6 us, or 1.093x.

The original gem5 ARM decoder lacks `FMOV Hd,Wn`, which GCC 11 emits in the
pre-ROI random initializer. The micro `common.hpp` and `common_spm.hpp` now
provide the opt-in `GEM5_ZERO_FP16_INPUT` compatibility mode. The classic-cache
comparison used that mode; it preserves allocation, memory geometry, and ROI
kernel control flow while changing only operand values to zero. Result paths:

- `paper_original_classic_vl2048_baseline_zero_init_1c_w7`
- `paper_original_classic_vl2048_spm_zero_init_1c_w7`

With the paper's non-prepacked `v1_fused`/`v3_fused_vl4` driver structure now
ported, fresh one-core W7 ROI totals are 1,681,210,000 ticks for baseline and
1,706,326,800 ticks for SPM, or 0.985x baseline performance. Both runs pass;
the SPM run issued and completed all 8,448 SPMCPs. These fresh directories use
the `derivo3paperdriverpf` tag. The remaining gap from the paper's 1.029x is
therefore not explained by its driver loop/packing structure; the most visible
remaining configuration difference is Ruby's stream prefetcher versus the
paper's classic-cache Stride/AMPM/BOP hierarchy (and its associated cache/bus
latencies).

The exact paper VL=16 W7 tile-shape binaries have also been built and run on
the one-core Ruby system. VL=16 uses the separate 24x1VL design (MT=24,
NT=128), KC=256, MC=784, one SPM load port, and four reserved SPM ways; it
must not be modeled by merely widening the VL=4 8x3VL binary. The baseline
completed at 703.73 GFLOP/s (584.1 us) and SPM at 768.90 GFLOP/s (534.6 us),
a 1.093x speedup. Both checksums were -1.1978825331 and all 8,192 SPMCPs
issued/completed. The paper reports about 1.172x for VL=16 W7, so Ruby
reproduces the direction and most, but not all, of the reported gain. The
reproducible runner is
`benchmarks/cacheflex_spm_gemm/run_paper_vl16_single_core.sh`.

The matched eight-core VL=16 kernel search now uses a 4M-by-2N thread grid for
both variants, a shared bit-exact NEON 24-row A packer, and two-way K-loop
software pipelining in both microkernels.  Sweeps of all factor pairs (1x8,
2x4, 4x2, and 8x1) selected 4x2 independently for baseline and SPM.  The final
clean W7 ROI results are 199,990,000 ticks for the coherent-cache baseline and
182,524,000 ticks for SPM, a 1.096x speedup (8.73% elapsed-time reduction).
Both checksums pass; SPM issued and completed 32,768 copies (4,096 per core).
Reproducible entry points are `build_vl16_best_baseline.sh`,
`build_vl16_best_spm.sh`, and `run_vl16_best_8core.sh` under
`benchmarks/cacheflex_spm_gemm`.

Nonzero functional validation no longer depends on guest-side FP16 random
conversion. `generate_fp16_correctness_input.py` writes deterministic A and B
matrices plus a complete host-computed FP16 C reference into the readfile.
The driver loads all three before the ROI and compares every one of W7's
802,816 outputs. `run_vl16_best_correctness_8core.sh baseline` and `spm` both
pass with zero maximum absolute error; the SPM run also issues/completes all
32,768 copies.

An 8-core VL=16 SPM driver now implements a fixed 2-by-4 output decomposition.
Thread `tid` owns the unique pair `(m_part=tid/4, n_part=tid%4)`.  Partitioning
is on the paper kernel's 24-by-128 tile boundaries: W7's 33 M tiles split as
16+17 and its eight N tiles split as two per N partition.  There are no inner
panel barriers.  Each B panel is therefore copied into two private SPMs (one
per M partition), not all eight.  The validated W7 run completed in 227,132,800
ROI ticks (227.133 us, 1,809.70 GFLOP/s), passed its full zero-output check, and
issued/completed 2,048 SPMCPs on every core (16,384 total) with no aliased
requests.  Sources and runners are `vl16_2m4n_driver.cpp`,
`build_vl16_2m4n.sh`, and `run_vl16_2m4n_8core.sh`; results are under
`results/cacheflex_spm_gemm/vl2048_spm_2m4n_ruby_8c_w7`.

The matching coherent-cache variant imports the paper's authoritative
`v1_24x1vl.cpp` cache microkernel into the same multicore driver.  It uses the
same 24-by-128 shape, 2-by-4 core ownership, A layout/packing, per-core B-panel
packing, synchronization, input placement, and ROI.  Only the B data path
differs: coherent packed-panel loads with all eight L2 ways versus SPMCP/SPMLD
with four ways reserved.  Its validated W7 ROI is 243,446,000 ticks
(243.446 us, 1,688.43 GFLOP/s), versus the SPM run's 227,132,800 ticks
(227.133 us, 1,809.70 GFLOP/s): 1.0718x speedup and 6.70% lower latency.
The baseline build/run scripts are `build_vl16_2m4n_baseline.sh` and
`run_vl16_2m4n_baseline_8core.sh`; results are in
`results/cacheflex_spm_gemm/vl2048_cache_2m4n_ruby_8c_w7`.

A second controlled pair now runs both paper-shaped kernels through ACL's
actual `NEScheduler` and `split_dimensions_all` path.  The shared custom
`ICPPKernel` exposes a 33-by-8 (M-tile by N-tile) window; ACL selects a 4M-by-2N
grid and its normal eight-thread CPP pool assigns the eight rectangles.  Both
variants log the resulting worker/window map and use identical ACL scheduling
overhead.  The coherent run is 365,266,400 ROI ticks (365.266 us); SPM is
335,344,400 ticks (335.344 us), a 1.0892x speedup and 8.19% lower latency.  Both
pass full output checking.  ACL's 4M-by-2N mapping makes every SPM core copy
four B panels, giving 4,096 issued/completed SPMCPs per core and 32,768 total.
Files are `vl16_acl_scheduler_driver.cpp`, `build_vl16_acl_scheduler.sh`, and
`run_vl16_acl_scheduler_8core.sh`.  Results use the
`vl2048_{cache,spm}_acl_scheduler_ruby_8c_w7` directories.  A cycle-debugging
workflow is documented in `docs/spm_cycle_debug.md`.

A full-stack upstream ACL FP16 baseline has now been built and run for W7 at
VL=16 with eight Ruby cores. The local harness only configures tensors,
requests eight threads, and marks ROI; ACL's unmodified `NEGEMM`, assembly
dispatch, packing, `NEScheduler`, and C++ thread pool perform the work. ACL
reports SVE=1, SVE2=0, and FP16=1. With `GEMMInfo::fast_math` enabled to select
ACL's SVE1 FP16-accumulate path, ROI is 293,666,800 ticks (293.667 us), or
1,399.69 GFLOP/s. The result directory is
`acl_fullstack_fp16_vl2048_ruby_8c_w7`; build and run instructions are in
`benchmarks/acl_full_stack_gemm/README.md`.

text:

```bash
cd /data2/rsappidi/cacheflex_mc

```

| 1 | 16,573,027 | 19,514,978 | 0.849x |

title: Correctness and comparison requirements
text:
- Baseline and SPM must use identical CPU, clock, cache geometry, SVE width,
  thread count, matrix dimensions, input placement, ROI boundaries, and
  statistics epochs. Only SPM enablement and the SPM kernel should differ.
- Always run both variants after a CPU or memory-system configuration change.
- Keep detailed chronological per-N-panel stats dumps.
- Confirm `GEMM_ROI begin`, normal work-end exit, and no Ruby panic before
  accepting a result.
- Check SPMCP issued/completed counts and outstanding-copy statistics.
- Check CPU cycles/instructions, cache misses, Ruby message classes, Garnet
  packets/flits/hops, directory traffic, and DRAM reads/writes.
- Do not interpret fewer L1 misses alone as a performance win.
- At multicore scale, explicitly account for each core independently copying
  the shared B panel.

title: Pending work
text:
### Additive W7 profiling counters

The VL=16 2M-by-4N SPM driver has an opt-in profiling build which uses
`m5_rpns()` to divide each thread's measured ROI into mutually exclusive
`pack_a`, `stage_b`, `kernel`, `loop_other`, and `final_wait` intervals.  Use
`benchmarks/cacheflex_spm_gemm/build_vl16_2m4n_profile.sh` and
`run_vl16_2m4n_profile_8core.sh`; the production binary is not overwritten.
The profile prints per-core `PHASE_CORE` records and aggregate-thread-time
`PHASE_SUM` records which add to exactly 100%.

The dedicated SPM LSQ also exports `spmRawBlockEvents`,
`spmRawBlockedUniqueLoads`, `spmRawWaitCycles`, `spmUnresolvedAddrRetries`,
`spmPortBlockedEvents`, `spmLoadResponses`, and `spmLoadServiceCycles` under
`system.cpuN.spmLsq0`.  Latency sums are per-load diagnostics and overlap in
time; do not add them to the phase percentages.

The verified 8-core VL=16 W7 profile is in
`results/cacheflex_spm_gemm/vl2048_spm_2m4n_profile_ruby_8c_w7`.  It passes and
reports 49.3576% pack A, 10.9355% stage B, 37.0370% kernel, 0.0382% loop other,
and 2.6317% final wait by aggregate thread-time.  The new LSQ counters show no
SPMCP RAW/address-resolution waits in this schedule, but 58,426 rejected SPM
load send attempts and 351,247 summed successful-send-to-response cycles over
67,587 responses.  The three extra core-7 responses beyond the static kernel
count should be treated as a diagnostic anomaly until classified.

The original guest pseudo-instruction kernel markers were removed because they
perturbed multicore scheduling.  Accurate kernel profiling now uses two
zero-byte assembler symbols in a labeled side binary to discover the existing
VL=16 assembly interval (`0x4014a8`--`0x401820`).  Simulation executes the
normal production ELF, not the labeled side binary.  Its `.text` section is
byte-for-byte identical to the labeled version.  The runner passes the PC
interval through `cacheFlexKernelStartPc`/`cacheFlexKernelEndPc`; O3 observes
the ROB head without inserting guest instructions.

O3 commit assigns every in-range cycle to exactly one of compute, SPM B data
movement, coherent-cache A data movement, C store/writeback, frontend/control,
or other-backend.  A progress cycle is classified from the most expensive
instruction class retiring that cycle; a zero-retirement cycle is classified
from the oldest ROB instruction blocking retirement.  This is a mutually
exclusive top-down attribution, not a sum of overlapping instruction
latencies.

The exact-production-ELF control and PC-profile runs both report 226,873,600
ROI ticks, 567,184 cycles per core, 622,463 injected Garnet packets, the same
exit tick, checksum, and SPMCP count.  The non-perturbing internal breakdown is
47.6380% compute, 9.5582% SPM B data movement, 42.5323% coherent-cache A data
movement, 0.1805% C store/writeback, 0.0533% frontend/control, and 0.0377%
other backend.  All bins sum exactly to 1,571,757 marked core-cycles.  The
result is `vl2048_spm_2m4n_pc_profile_ruby_8c_w7`; reproduce the table with
`scripts/analyze_kernel_cycles.py <result>/stats.txt`.

The identical matched-driver cache baseline now has the same zero-overhead PC
profiling.  Its production and symbol-only side binary `.text` sections are
byte-identical (SHA-256 `37787a08ffeb4a9444bd5db540b07d75cdc4c7afeec6600c1c1acbe2dd93af9d`).
The full kernel interval is `0x400e00`--`0x401134`; the cache B `ld1h` is
`0x400ea0`--`0x400ea4`, allowing regular-cache A and B attribution to remain
separate.  Control and profile both report 248,290,400 ROI ticks, 620,726
cycles/core, 646,840 Garnet packets, the same exit tick, and PASS.  The
baseline kernel breakdown is 49.7118% compute, 29.9994% cache A movement,
19.9706% cache B movement, 0.1266% C store/writeback, 0.1831%
frontend/control, and 0.0085% other backend; the 1,510,633 classified cycles
sum exactly.  The result is `vl2048_cache_2m4n_pc_profile_ruby_8c_w7`.

A separate `CACHEFLEX_VL16_PIPELINED` SPM variant now implements an explicit
two-way K pipeline.  It alternates B in `z2`/`z3` and A in
`{z0,z1,z5}`/`{z4,z6,z7}` while retaining `z8`--`z31` as the 24 accumulators;
an odd-K cleanup path is included.  The paper-matched non-pipelined binary is
unchanged.  The normal and symbol-only optimized binaries have byte-identical
`.text` (SHA-256 `63acadb7214ec1517f9be82d23a835f2295cab45655eee16ed68025cf0160489`).

The optimized 8-core W7 run passes with all 16,384 SPMCPs and takes
222,886,400 ROI ticks, versus 226,873,600 for the previous SPM kernel and
248,290,400 for the matched cache baseline.  This is 1.0179x over the old SPM
implementation and 1.1140x over baseline (10.2316% lower latency).  Its exact
PC profile matches the unprofiled run and classifies 1,503,051 kernel
core-cycles: 46.0196% compute, 43.7077% cache A, 9.8732% SPM B, 0.1973% C
stores, 0.1617% frontend/control, and 0.0405% other backend.  Result paths are
`vl2048_spm_2m4n_pipelined_ruby_8c_w7` and
`vl2048_spm_2m4n_pipelined_pc_profile_ruby_8c_w7`.

Multicast SPMCP is now implemented without replacing the original path.
Destination operand bits 31:24 carry an eight-core mask; the leader performs
one coherent fetch, installs locally, sends one Garnet multicast data message,
and completes only after acknowledgements from every selected private L1.
Dynamic SPM slot preparation is atomic: a coherent occupant is migrated when
space exists, otherwise normal coherent replacement is triggered, and the
selected physical way is protected from intervening coherent fills until
installation. Scalar SPMLD decoding was completed so the multicast kernel can
use address-aware completion markers.

The separate multicast kernel uses a 4-M by 2-N mapping, bootstraps the first
panel through the preserved single-destination path, then shares subsequent B
panels within each N group. A 256-row staging window was fastest among 16, 64,
and 256; 2-M by 4-N was also tested and was slower. Fresh correctness-checked
W7 results on the same rebuilt gem5 are: baseline 204,632,800 ROI ticks,
non-multicast SPM 164,370,000, and multicast SPM 161,166,800. Thus multicast
is 1.270x over baseline and 1.020x over the refreshed non-multicast SPM. It
issues/completes 14,336 SPMCPs versus 32,768 for non-multicast. Result paths
end in `cache_best_correctness_multicastgem5_8c_w7`,
`spm_best_correctness_multicastgem5_8c_w7`, and
`spm_multicast_commit_w256_correct_8c_w7`.

FlashAttention now has a separately built receiver-ready multicast kernel,
`spm_konly_multicast_ready`.  Ruby sends `SPM_MCAST_PENDING` before fetching a
multicast source line; each selected receiver atomically prepares the target
slot in the transient `XP` state.  Local SPMLD/SPMST requests stall in `XP`
until `SPM_MCAST_DATA` installs the line and wakes the request, so the leader no
longer needs a barrier or installation acknowledgements for each future panel.
The optimized software uses private per-core copies for the first K panel to
avoid leader-serialized startup, then double-buffers subsequent K panels and
multicasts them asynchronously.  The private-copy and barrier-based multicast
kernels remain available as controls.  At 8 cores, VL=4, Br=64, Bc=96, the
hybrid kernel is bit-exact and takes 61,796,000 ROI ticks at T=128 and
152,539,000 ticks at T=256.  The pre-hybrid receiver-ready results were
64,679,000 and 154,363,000 ticks, respectively.  Result directories are
`spm_konly_multicast_hybrid_final_t128` and
`spm_konly_multicast_hybrid_t256`.

The three-line `SPMCPB3_64` instruction now uses one architectural instruction
and one SPM-LSQ entry.  That entry fans out three coherent 64-byte Ruby SPMCP
transactions from consecutive source lines to ways 0, 1, and 2, and aggregates
all three responses before releasing the address-aware shadow-table entry.
The original scalar SPMCP path remains unchanged.  The FlashAttention variant
is `spm_konly_multicast_ready_batch3`; its true-LSQ result directories end in
`batch3_lsq_t128` and `batch3_lsq_t256`.  Both runs are bit-exact and complete
every Ruby transaction, but take 63,070,000 and 158,664,000 ROI ticks versus
61,796,000 and 152,539,000 for the scalar hybrid.  Thus the current batch is
2.06% and 4.02% slower.  It removes frontend/LSQ command overhead but does not
reduce Ruby traffic, and treating three lines as one scheduling unit reduces
the instruction-level overlap available to the scalar sequence.  A faster
follow-on needs a decoupled internal copy queue that accepts the batch command
once and issues its component lines independently while later batches proceed.

A decoupled two-dimensional SPM DMA is now implemented on the active branch;
the pre-extension reference is preserved as branch
`cacheflex-multicore-reference` at commit `bcff1e627581caa22587815c6c9e12b4ed70867a`.
`SPMDMA_2D_64 xDesc, [xSrc]` encodes destination set/way, row count, lines per
row, source stride, and optional eight-core multicast mask in `xDesc`. One
architectural store/SQ entry launches the command; after the first accepted
line it retires while `LSQ::activeDmas` emits one component line per cycle via
the existing SPM port and Ruby SPMCP protocol. All responses aggregate before
the address-aware shadow entry becomes ready. Draining and CPU takeover also
account for active DMA commands. The blocked-store retry path must register a
DMA after its first line is eventually accepted; omitting this caused the
initial V-panel completion deadlock. In SE mode every generated virtual source
line is translated independently through the process page table. Translating
only the base silently corrupted transfers crossing noncontiguous physical
pages.

FlashAttention variant `spm_kv_dma_pinall` uses one 64-row by three-line DMA
per K block and one `Bc`-row by two-line DMA per V panel, retaining the
six-way pinned K/V multicast layout. Correctness-checked 8-core VL=4 results
are 69,549,000 ROI ticks at T=128 and 173,410,000 at T=256, with hashes
`78b397aeae450383` and `e91cc35851f10383` and zero nonfinite outputs. At T=256
this is 1.0236x faster than the equivalent scalar line-copy pinned-K/V result
(177,498,000 ticks), but remains slower than K-only staging (146,582,000
ticks). Results are `spm_kv_dma_pinall_final_t128` and
`spm_kv_dma_pinall_final_t256`.

A broader DMA/FlashAttention solution sweep subsequently tested scalar versus
DMA staging, receiver-ready overlap versus pin-all, Br={32,64,128},
Bc={64,96,128}, 1/2/4/8 DMA injection ports, ROB={128,256,384,512,640,768,1024}
with proportionally enlarged IQ/LQ/SQ, 16 cache/SPM load ports, 256 sequencer
outstanding requests, 4 MiB L0D, 4 MiB private L2, and one-cycle SIMD latency.
Every accepted result was checked against the expected hash and for nonfinite
outputs. Bc=128 was rejected because the current 96-column kernel reads a
partial second block and changed the hash. The 4 MiB private-L2 experiments
were rejected because the current SPM canonical-address mapping assumes the
paper cache geometry and panicked on a set mismatch.

The sweep exposed and fixed an important software error: K-only kernels were
still claiming and draining the unused two-way V layout inside the ROI.
`claim_layout` and `claim_pinned_kv` now condition claims and drains on
`CACHEFLEX_FLASH_STAGE_K/V`. The best correct DMA point uses K-only
receiver-ready multicast, interleaved query blocks, four regular-LSQ/DMA store
injection ports, ROB/IQ/LQ/SQ=768/480/192/288. It takes 55,904,000 ticks at
T=128 and 132,979,000 at T=256. Increasing to eight injection ports or a 1024
entry ROB regresses. Pinning all K panels also regresses. Results are
`noclaimv_win768_w4_t128` and `noclaimv_win768_w4_t256`.

This is only 1.0475x over the identically enlarged cache baseline at T=128
(58,559,000 ticks) and 1.0963x at T=256 (145,787,000 ticks). On the paper core,
K-only scalar and DMA are 141,761,000 and 140,610,000 ticks at T=256; widening
only DMA/store injection to four ports reaches 138,154,000. Thus the tested
transport, capacity, tiling, overlap, and core-resource changes do not reveal
a large remaining CacheFlex-specific gain. The limiting work is the dependent
QK/online-softmax/PV dataflow; a materially larger improvement requires
algorithmic fusion or new compute support, not another SPMCP transport tweak.

A controlled FlashAttention bottleneck sweep was run on the validated scalar
receiver-ready multicast kernel.  At T=128 the 61.796M-tick control falls to
60.627M with ROB=512 alone, 61.370M with IQ=320 alone, 61.533M with 4x LQ/SQ,
58.832M with all four window structures enlarged, 61.066M with 16 cache/SPM
load ports plus 256 Ruby outstanding requests, 58.259M with both idealizations,
and 58.522M when all SIMD arithmetic/reduction latencies are set to one cycle.
At T=256, the 152.539M control falls to 148.082M with the large window and
145.841M with one-cycle SIMD.  All checksums/hashes pass.  The T=128 control
has only 10 SPM RAW blocks (817 summed wait cycles), 34 SPM-port rejects, and
5.20-cycle average SPM-load service over 49,162 responses, but 37,110 ROB-full
events.  This bounds further SPMCP/SPMLD acceleration to a small gain in the
current dataflow; the primary limits are dependent SIMD work and insufficient
lookahead across that work, not copy traffic.  The runner exposes
`CACHEFLEX_FLASH_IDEAL_SIMD`, L0D size/associativity, and the existing window,
port, and sequencer environment controls for reproducing these ablations.

The resulting FlashAttention optimization is
`spm_konly_multicast_ready_interleave`.  The existing j-outer kernel already
reused each staged K/V panel across all local query blocks, so the new variant
adds the missing instruction-level independence: it materializes separate S/P
scratch regions for the query blocks, separates their QK/softmax/PV phases, and
evaluates two softmax rows in lockstep to expose independent max, exp, and sum
chains.  The old receiver-ready kernel remains unchanged as a control.  Final
bit-exact 8-core results are 58.506M ROI ticks at T=128 and 141.235M at T=256,
versus the previous best SPM results of 61.796M and 152.539M (1.056x and 1.080x
kernel speedups).  Matched rebuilt cache results are 68.982M and 165.751M, so
the optimized CacheFlex speedups are 1.179x and 1.174x.  Result directories end
in `interleave_qblocks_rows2_final_t128`,
`interleave_qblocks_rows2_final_t256`, `interleave_matched_cache_t128`, and
`interleave_matched_cache_t256`.

A T=256 SPM-way/residency sweep was also completed with one fixed binary build.
For the optimized K-only receiver-ready kernel, configuring 3, 4, 6, or 8
dynamic SPM ways gives exactly the same 146.582M ROI ticks and bit-exact hash,
because software occupies only ways 0--2 and unclaimed eligible ways remain
normal coherent capacity.  A new `spm_kv_multicast_pinall` control uses six
ways: persistent K in ways 0--2 and persistent V in ways 4--5.  It is correct,
but both the 6- and 8-way configurations take 177.498M ticks.  Relative to
K-only, pinning V reduces L0D misses from 94,170 to 90,923 (3.4%) but increases
private-L2 misses from 33,549 to 40,980 (22.2%) and injected packets from
155,600 to 220,304 (41.6%).  Thus increasing the configured way ceiling is
free when ways are unused, but full V residency is counterproductive in the
current design because claim/install traffic and lost coherent capacity exceed
the saved V demand traffic.  Result directories use
`waysweep_konly_w{3,4,6,8}_t256` and `waysweep_kvpin_w{6,8}_t256`.

1. Complete and verify the server build after the two compatibility fixes.
2. Run one-core baseline and SPM smoke tests.
3. Validate shadow-table correctness without `DSB SY` using SPMCP issued versus
   completed counts and the absence of stale-data/protocol failures.
4. Run the new DerivO3 1/2/4/8-core W7 sweep.
5. Compare per-epoch cycles and traffic with the historical Neoverse run, but
   keep the configurations clearly separated.
6. Port and validate the micro FP16 VL=8 and VL=16 tile-specific kernels in
   the multicore harness.
7. Only after the single-SPMCP design is stable, evaluate a batch/multicast
   instruction that copies one coherent source line to multiple private SPMs.

title: Repository safety
text:
- This worktree contains user work and substantial protocol modifications.
  Do not reset, checkout, or overwrite unrelated files.
- Do not replace Ruby protocol files from `cacheflex_micro`; doing so would
  discard the multicore extension.
- When resolving imported-O3 build errors, prefer narrow compatibility changes
  and document each one in this file.
- Do not reintroduce SNAP/move semantics unless explicitly requested. The
  current target is the original single-copy SPMCP behavior.
- Do not rerun long baselines unless the configuration changed or the user asks
  for them. The current DerivO3 change does require new baselines.
